content.text:
The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "The Generational Legacy of Samples in Music": https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/
The files: data/songs.csv, data/samples.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data folder and reading the story.

content.text:
Title: How Sonic DNA Connects Generations of Music
URL Source: https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/
Published Time: Mon, 06 Jul 2026 15:03:28 GMT
Markdown Content:
[Skip to main content](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/#content)
[![Image 1: pudding logo](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/secondary.png)](https://pudding.cool/)
![Image 2: An illustration of a network visualization showing album covers connected by lines.](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/tree.jpg)
# This is a project about shared DNA in music.
Loading visualization data...
A quick note, if you are using a screen reader, use the left and right arrow keys to navigate between slides. Now back to the story.
What if today’s most iconic sounds aren’t just from today…
Visual description: A vertical chain begins with I Believe to My Soul by Ray Charles and continues to I Believe to My Soul by Monk Higgins.
...but are inherited from a family of sound…
Visual description: The vertical chain connects I Believe to My Soul by Monk Higgins to Not Like Us by Kendrick Lamar.
# How sound is passed down over generations
#### By [Stephen Lurie](https://pudding.cool/author/stephen-lurie/). Graphics by [Jared Whalen](https://pudding.cool/author/jared-whalen/)
Some musical inheritance is pretty obvious, because it shares iconic sounds, such as the bass from “Under Pressure,” which was transformed into “Ice Ice Baby.”
Visual description: A vertical chain links Under Pressure by Queen & David Bowie to Ice Ice Baby by Vanilla Ice.
But many songs have a far more complex and concealed musical history, spanning genres, cultures, and even centuries.
Let’s trace the family history of one.
Orchestral music for a play in 1875 becomes electronic music for a cartoon in 1983.
Visual description: The vertical chain connects In the Hall of the Mountain King by Edvard Grieg to Inspector Gadget by Haim Saban.
Which is transformed by a minor rap group...
Visual description: The vertical chain extends from Inspector Gadget by Haim Saban to Bad Boys by Bad Boys.
...which then presents a rap giant with the lyrics to start his breakout hit…
Visual description: The vertical chain continues to Big Poppa by The Notorious B.I.G..
...which connects to a chain of lyrical references in the diss tracks of the rap rivalry between Biggie Smalls and Tupac Shakur.
Finally, in 1996, over 120 years after “In the Hall of the Mountain King,” 2pac released the song at the end of this musical lineage, “Hit ’Em Up”“Hit ’Em Up”.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues through Conspiracy by Junior M.A.F.I.A. and ends with How Do U Want It by 2Pac.
“Hit ’Em Up’s” lineage depicts the many kinds of musical DNA that's passed down, over time. In this example, each generation is connected by a sample—where a song reuses part of an original recording—or an interpolation—where a song uses a re-recording of sound.
Visual description: The vertical chain maps a musical family tree from Edvard Grieg in 1895 down through a series of sampled tracks, ending with 2Pac’s How Do U Want It in 1996.
This isn’t “Hit ’Em Up’s” only lineage, but one of many, connected through samples, interpolations, covers and remixes.
Another lineage begins with the smooth R&B passed down from Dionne Warwick’s “Walk on By.” Next, Isaac Hayes reinterprets the song and slows down the tempo.
Visual description: The view zooms to another lineage, beginning with Walk on By by Dionne Warwick and continuing to Walk on By by Isaac Hayes.
This catches the ear of Biggie Smalls and forms the basis of his track “Warning”...
Visual description: The vertical chain continues to Warning by The Notorious B.I.G..
…and just a few more generations below “Warning” is once again, “Hit ’Em Up.”
Visual description: The vertical chain branches and converges as both lineages—one through Warning, the other through Junior M.A.F.I.A.—lead back to 2Pac’s Hit ’Em Up at the bottom.
And there’s the soul of Tom Jones’ “Looking Out My Window.” Brooklyn rap group Stetsasonic brings Tom Jones’ drums into rap rhythms.
Visual description: The view zooms to another lineage, connecting Looking Out My Window by Tom Jones to Go Stetsa I by Stetsasonic.
Stetsasonic’s iconic line “Go Brooklyn” sets out a chain of beats, and lyrics set to those beats, that leads again to “Hit ’Em Up.”
Visual description: The vertical chain branches from Go Stetsa I by Stetsasonic to Top Billin’ by Audio Two and Lyte as a Rock by MC Lyte, forming a beat-driven path that loops back to 2Pac’s Hit ’Em Up.
And, crucially, there’s the funk of “Blind Man Can See It” by James Brown, one of the “grandparents” of “Hit ’Em Up” from a different line. This iconic bass riff is a clear influence on the bassline of Dennis Edwards and Siedah Garrett’s “Don’t Look Any Further.”
Visual description: The vertical chain shifts to linking James Brown’s Blind Man Can See It to Don’t Look Any Further by Dennis Edwards.
“Hit ’Em Up” then samples “Don’t Look Any Further’s” bassline.
Visual description: The vertical chain completes with Hit ’Em Up by 2Pac, linking back to the bassline of Don’t Look Any Further by Dennis Edwards.
That’s four branches building up to this one song.
Visual description: A full view of the vertical chain reveals four musical branches—spanning orchestral, soul, funk, and hip-hop—converging on 2Pac’s Hit ’Em Up.
This DNA is made up of borrowed beats, loaned lyrics, and multipurpose melodies.
Visual description: Highlighted paths are added to the tree that trace melody, beats, and lyrics through key tracks—each strand of musical DNA leading into the final form of Hit ’Em Up.
All of this is just a fraction of the full DNA; each of these songs also have their own origins.
Altogether, “Hit ’Em Up” is the descendent of a larger history, a culmination of an 82-song family tree (the branches we’ve already explored are highlighted).
Some of “Hit ’Em Up’s” ancestors are directly audible in the final product; others are not. But all of these tracks were influences, big and small, in the generational development of “Hit ’Em Up.”
Visual description: The view zooms out to reveal the full 82-song family tree, with highlighted branches tracing the direct lineage that leads to 2Pac’s Hit ’Em Up.
![Image 3: A stylized title for the Musical cousins section.](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/headers/music.png)
### When we consider samples, remixes, interpolations, and covers as musical family ties, we can trace how the DNA of one song can spread across genres and cultures. We can see how very different songs might actually be related.
Let’s return to the lineage between “In the Hall of the Mountain King” and “Big Poppa.”
Visual description: A vertical chain retraces the path from In the Hall of the Mountain King to Big Poppa.
The descendants of “In the Hall of the Mountain King” include Jhene Aiko’s The Worst The Worst, a great-great-great grandchild of “In the Hall of the Mountain King” due to a shared lineage with “Big Poppa.”
Visual description: The vertical chain extends from In the Hall of the Mountain King through a shared lineage with Big Poppa, eventually reaching The Worst by Jhené Aiko.
But if we take a different route through the family tree, we can even see “In the Hall of the Mountain King” make its way to Korean rap in J-Hope’s song “What if…”
Visual description: The vertical chain follows an alternate route from In the Hall of the Mountain King to What if by J-Hope, tracing a lineage that spans from classical music to Korean rap.
Doug E. Fresh samples the familiar riff from Inspector Gadget.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues as The Show by Doug E. Fresh & The Get Fresh Crew builds on the riff from Inspector Gadget, blending it into a new hip-hop classic.
Slick Rick’s lyrics are then copied by Big Daddy Kane on “Show & Prove.”
Visual description: The vertical chain continues as Show & Prove by Big Daddy Kane echoes lyrics from The Show
Ol' Dirty Bastard then repeats his own lyrics on “Shimmy Shimmy Ya.”
Visual description: The vertical chain continues with Shimmy Shimmy Ya by Ol’ Dirty Bastard.
J-Hope reinterprets the riff from “Shimmy Shimmy Ya” on the track “What if…”
Visual description: The vertical chain concludes with What if... by j-hope.
The branch to “What if...” is just one of the many, many cousins of “Hit ’Em Up” within “In the Hall of the Mountain King’s” family tree.
If we zoom out, we can see them all, and how “In The Hall of the Mountain King” affects music across 5 generations and 833 songs.
Visual description: The view zooms out to reveal a vast, circular web of 833 songs, with highlighted branches tracing the path from In the Hall of the Mountain King to both What if... and Hit 'Em Up.
The connections in these musical family trees may be a borrowed beat, loaned lyrics, or a multipurpose melody.
Let’s look at examples of each one.
![Image 4: A stylized title for the Borrowed beats section.](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/headers/beats.png)
Some songs have introduced beats that have directly been sampled by hundreds, or even thousands, of other songs.
Depicted here are a small fraction of songs that sample or interpolate James Brown’s 1970 track “Funky Drummer,” which is used in everything from George Michael’s Freedom! '90 Freedom! '90, to Alanis Morissette’s Head Over Feet Head Over Feet, to Ed Sheeran’s Shirtsleeves Shirtsleeves.
And once you hear it, you’ll hear it everywhere; the “Funky Drummer” has been used in thousands of songs and has the most “descendants” in music history.
Visual description: A towering cascade of connections flows from James Brown’s Funky Drummer.
Because the beat doesn’t just pass down to one generation.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues from Funky Drummer to South Bronx by Boogie Down Productions.
It leads “South Bronx” to shape the sound of another Bronx artist’s hit.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues as South Bronx influences Jenny from the Block by Jennifer Lopez.
“Jenny From the Block” is only one of a whole second generation of songs that originate from Clyde Stubblefield’s improvised drum break 5 minutes and 35 seconds into “Funky Drummer.” There’s also Will Smith’s Wild Wild West Wild Wild West, The Power The Power by SNAP!, Rub You The Right Way Rub You The Right Way by Johnny Gill.
Visual description: A zoomed-out view of a branching network from Funky Drummer, with highlighted paths tracing second-generation descendants like Jenny From the Block and dozens of other genre-spanning hits.
![Image 5: A stylized title for the Loaned lyrics section.](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/headers/lyrics.png)
While a beat sets the foundation for a song, lyrics are some of the most easily transmittable DNA: a few words can easily fit into otherwise very different songs.
Here's an example of lyrics slightly evolving through generations: A Tribe Called Quest released “Can I Kick It?” in 1990, itself a song built on Lou Reed’s “Walk on the Wild Side” from 1972. When Q-Tip asks if he can kick it, the rest of the Tribe responds.
Visual description: A vertical chain begins with Can I Kick It? by A Tribe Called Quest.
Robbie Williams then used the line in 2000’s “Rock DJ.” Williams [said](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BnaPtu2sshs) he, “Really struggled to write the lyrics. So what I’ve just done is I’ve robbed loads of really old rap lyrics.”
But instead of his own band responding, it now sounds like the DJ’s crowd.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues to Rock DJ by Robbie Williams.
In 2021, Lorde picked up the line [from](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=If-VG2s0lX8) Robbie Williams— not A Tribe Called Quest—but she takes on both parts.
Visual description: The vertical chain reaches Solar Power by Lorde.
The structure of a catchy phrase can also produce variations with different content altogether.
Tupac also used the phrase “I keep my mind on my money, money on my mind” in a verse on MC Breed’s 1993 Gotta Get Mine Gotta Get Mine, but it blew up when Snoop Dogg quoted it in the chorus of “Gin and Juice” later that year.
Visual description: A branching chain from Snoop Dogg’s Doggystyle to songs by Rihanna and Demi Lovato.
Demi Lovato’s “Cool for the Summer” (2015) plays with that line, but shifts the focus in a different direction…
Visual description: The vertical chain continues from Snoop Dogg’s Gin and Juice to Demi Lovato’s Cool for the Summer.
While Rihanna’s “Cheers (Drink to That)” from 2010, in addition to heavily sampling Avril Lavigne’s “I’m With You,” abandons the parallel format entirely…
Visual description: The vertical chain also leads to Cheers (Drink to That) by Rihanna.
Or the words can stay exactly the same, but completely change meaning.
Chubby Checker popularized the phrase “How low can you go” when he added vocals to The Champs’ song “Limbo Rock.” He’s asking about how far to lower the limbo stick…
Visual description: The vertical chain follows the phrase “How low can you go” from its limbo origins in Limbo Rock to new meanings in tracks by Public Enemy, Ludacris, and Charley Crockett.
But then Chuck D uses the line to talk about the bass singing register.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues to Bring the Noise by Public Enemy.
Ludacris then samples Chuck D’s voice from “Bring the Noise” and alters the tempo and quality to kick off his 2010 song “How Low,” where he’s talking about “booty.”
Visual description: The vertical chain continues to How Low by Ludacris.
While we don’t know which lyric inspired Charley Crockett for his 2019 record “How Low Can You Go,” Crockett used the phrase to describe what a romantic interest is doing to his heart.
Visual description: The vertical chain lands on How Low Can You Go by Charley Crockett.
![Image 6: A stylized title for the Multipurpose melodies section.](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/headers/melodies.png)
For most people, however, melody is the most identifiable kind of musical DNA. Sampled and interpolated melodies may be instantly recognizable, hit on a subconscious familiarity even if you’re not aware there’s a sample at all, or sit right at the edge of recognition, making you think “where have I heard that before?”
While sampling is commonly associated with hip hop, the art of sharing and borrowing melodies is a global practice, transcending every genre.
For example, where does this international selection of hits get their sound?
Visual description: Four modern songs—Shaky Shaky by Daddy Yankee, Freaks by French Montana, Post to Be by Omarion, and Labios Mordidos by Kali Uchis and Karol G —are arranged in a horizontal row.
The immediate answer is the 1992 classic “Murder She Wrote” by Chaka Demus and Pliers.
Visual description: A visual tree forms showing the influence of Murder She Wrote by Chaka Demus & Pliers (1992) on the four modern songs.
But “Murder She Wrote” is actually only one of many songs based on a sound from 1973. The bouncing melody behind the song comes from a “riddim”—the instrumental pattern in reggae and dancehall music—that emerged from the song “Stalag 17.”
Visual description: The visual tree shows the instrumental lineage from Stalag 17 by Dave & Ansel Collins (1973) down to Murder She Wrote by Chaka Demus & Pliers (1992), which then branches to the four modern songs.
The “Stalag Riddim” and its descendants form the basis for countless Jamaican hits, including “Murder She Wrote” and Sister Nancy’s “Bam Bam.”
Visual description: The tree highlights how the "Stalag Riddim" from Stalag 17 by Dave & Ansel Collins (1973) leads to Bam Bam by Sister Nancy (1982). Below, Murder She Wrote by Chaka Demus & Pliers (1992) and the four modern songs
Descendants of “Bam Bam” include songs like Do to Me Do to Me by H.E.R., Lost Ones Lost Ones by Lauryn Hill, and Bam Bam by Jay-Z and Damian Marley.
Once a melody enters our musical family in this way, the original source can fade into obscurity, even as the sound continues to pass on and evolve. The descendents of this current generation of songs will build on a melody that a few Jamaican studio musicians recorded in 1973, even if they’ve never given them a second of thought.
Visual description: The tree then traces the influence of Stalag 17 through Bam Bam to three newer songs: Do to Me by H.E.R. (2020), Bam by JAY-Z (2017), and Lost Ones by Lauryn Hill (1998).
# Not your grandparents’ samples
Sampling has become so widespread and so sophisticated, that you can have hits that not only have a wide range of ancestors—they also actually sound like those ancestors. Artists and producers can create incredibly complex and catchy sounds, drawing from a wide range of sources.
Let’s look at the song “Shake It” by Kay Flock featuring Cardi B, Dougie B, and Bory 300. This sample heavy song took off on TikTok before it was even released, and then was one of the New York Times’ top songs of 2022.
Visual description: A visual tree that traces the musical influences behind Shake It by Kay Flock, Cardi B & Dougie B (2022), dividing them into three source tracks: melody from Temperature by Sean Paul, lyrics from Bananza (Belly Dancer) by Akon, and bass from Is Ya Ready by Kay Flock.
In just this segment, there’s a tune from Buffalo Springfield Buffalo Springfield and Fun Boy Three Fun Boy Three, background vocals from Akon’s Bananza Bananza, a clap beat from Sean Paul’s Temperature Temperature and an earlier riddim, and a bass line from a previous Kay Flock song Is Ya Ready Is Ya Ready, all combined together.
The song, produced by Elias Beats, also represents how generational and cross-genre sampling has been turbocharged. Beatmakers like Elias Beats now produce sample-based beats and post them online for free for anyone to build a song around. His YouTube channel has drill beats built around everything from [“Hips Don’t Lie”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x1e4FEaU2xk) to “Just Dance” to [“I Want it That Way”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MyjCpyYgs40) or [“Gangnam Style.”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CjqaJjZ1zSY) Diverse musical DNA from all kinds of traditions and genres are being mixed up and spread out in new and surprising ways.
Then again–there’s something to sticking to the classics, too.
Visual description: A vertical chain connects Ice Ice Baby by Vanilla Ice to Bops Goin Brazy by Tyga.
Methodology To build this project, we used the dataset of hundreds of thousands of songs on Genius.com accessible through their API, over 200,000 of which were “connected” in some way by sample, interpolation, cover, or remix. We used this dataset to identify promising examples and then confirmed or revised the relationships in those examples based on cross-checking with other sources, including WhoSampled.com, Spotify, and news media and academic scholarship. The financial, legal, and reputational implications of sampling and interpolation mean that while reproducing or imitating sound is sometimes formally acknowledged by artists, many others times it is not. The connections we propose here are our interpretation, based on one or more of acknowledged credits by the artists, third-party interpretation, or the sonic evidence available to us.Thank you to DJ LoBraico, Ben Talmi, Josh Katz, and Larry Buchanan for sharing some of their technical and musical skill with this project.

Title: How Sonic DNA Connects Generations of Music
URL Source: https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/?x-respond-with=html
Markdown Content:

[![Image 3: pudding logo](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/secondary.png)](https://pudding.cool/)
![Image 4: An illustration of a network visualization showing album covers connected by lines.](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/tree.jpg)
# This is a project about shared DNA in music.
Begin (with music!)Stay Muted
A quick note, if you are using a screen reader, use the left and right arrow keys to navigate between slides. Now back to the story.
What if today’s most iconic sounds aren’t just from today…
Visual description: A vertical chain begins with I Believe to My Soul by Ray Charles and continues to I Believe to My Soul by Monk Higgins.
...but are inherited from a family of sound…
Visual description: The vertical chain connects I Believe to My Soul by Monk Higgins to Not Like Us by Kendrick Lamar.
# How sound is passed down over generations
#### By [Stephen Lurie](https://pudding.cool/author/stephen-lurie/). Graphics by [Jared Whalen](https://pudding.cool/author/jared-whalen/)
Some musical inheritance is pretty obvious, because it shares iconic sounds, such as the bass from “Under Pressure,” which was transformed into “Ice Ice Baby.”
Visual description: A vertical chain links Under Pressure by Queen & David Bowie to Ice Ice Baby by Vanilla Ice.
But many songs have a far more complex and concealed musical history, spanning genres, cultures, and even centuries.
Let’s trace the family history of one.
Orchestral music for a play in 1875 becomes electronic music for a cartoon in 1983.
Visual description: The vertical chain connects In the Hall of the Mountain King by Edvard Grieg to Inspector Gadget by Haim Saban.
Which is transformed by a minor rap group...
Visual description: The vertical chain extends from Inspector Gadget by Haim Saban to Bad Boys by Bad Boys.
...which then presents a rap giant with the lyrics to start his breakout hit…
Visual description: The vertical chain continues to Big Poppa by The Notorious B.I.G..
...which connects to a chain of lyrical references in the diss tracks of the rap rivalry between Biggie Smalls and Tupac Shakur.
Finally, in 1996, over 120 years after “In the Hall of the Mountain King,” 2pac released the song at the end of this musical lineage, “Hit ’Em Up”“Hit ’Em Up”.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues through Conspiracy by Junior M.A.F.I.A. and ends with How Do U Want It by 2Pac.
“Hit ’Em Up’s” lineage depicts the many kinds of musical DNA that's passed down, over time. In this example, each generation is connected by a sample—where a song reuses part of an original recording—or an interpolation—where a song uses a re-recording of sound.
Visual description: The vertical chain maps a musical family tree from Edvard Grieg in 1895 down through a series of sampled tracks, ending with 2Pac’s How Do U Want It in 1996.
This isn’t “Hit ’Em Up’s” only lineage, but one of many, connected through samples, interpolations, covers and remixes.
Another lineage begins with the smooth R&B passed down from Dionne Warwick’s “Walk on By.” Next, Isaac Hayes reinterprets the song and slows down the tempo.
Visual description: The view zooms to another lineage, beginning with Walk on By by Dionne Warwick and continuing to Walk on By by Isaac Hayes.
This catches the ear of Biggie Smalls and forms the basis of his track “Warning”...
Visual description: The vertical chain continues to Warning by The Notorious B.I.G..
…and just a few more generations below “Warning” is once again, “Hit ’Em Up.”
Visual description: The vertical chain branches and converges as both lineages—one through Warning, the other through Junior M.A.F.I.A.—lead back to 2Pac’s Hit ’Em Up at the bottom.
And there’s the soul of Tom Jones’ “Looking Out My Window.” Brooklyn rap group Stetsasonic brings Tom Jones’ drums into rap rhythms.
Visual description: The view zooms to another lineage, connecting Looking Out My Window by Tom Jones to Go Stetsa I by Stetsasonic.
Stetsasonic’s iconic line “Go Brooklyn” sets out a chain of beats, and lyrics set to those beats, that leads again to “Hit ’Em Up.”
Visual description: The vertical chain branches from Go Stetsa I by Stetsasonic to Top Billin’ by Audio Two and Lyte as a Rock by MC Lyte, forming a beat-driven path that loops back to 2Pac’s Hit ’Em Up.
And, crucially, there’s the funk of “Blind Man Can See It” by James Brown, one of the “grandparents” of “Hit ’Em Up” from a different line. This iconic bass riff is a clear influence on the bassline of Dennis Edwards and Siedah Garrett’s “Don’t Look Any Further.”
Visual description: The vertical chain shifts to linking James Brown’s Blind Man Can See It to Don’t Look Any Further by Dennis Edwards.
“Hit ’Em Up” then samples “Don’t Look Any Further’s” bassline.
Visual description: The vertical chain completes with Hit ’Em Up by 2Pac, linking back to the bassline of Don’t Look Any Further by Dennis Edwards.
That’s four branches building up to this one song.
Visual description: A full view of the vertical chain reveals four musical branches—spanning orchestral, soul, funk, and hip-hop—converging on 2Pac’s Hit ’Em Up.
This DNA is made up of borrowed beats, loaned lyrics, and multipurpose melodies.
Visual description: Highlighted paths are added to the tree that trace melody, beats, and lyrics through key tracks—each strand of musical DNA leading into the final form of Hit ’Em Up.
All of this is just a fraction of the full DNA; each of these songs also have their own origins.
Altogether, “Hit ’Em Up” is the descendent of a larger history, a culmination of an 82-song family tree (the branches we’ve already explored are highlighted).
Some of “Hit ’Em Up’s” ancestors are directly audible in the final product; others are not. But all of these tracks were influences, big and small, in the generational development of “Hit ’Em Up.”
Visual description: The view zooms out to reveal the full 82-song family tree, with highlighted branches tracing the direct lineage that leads to 2Pac’s Hit ’Em Up.
![Image 5: A stylized title for the Musical cousins section.](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/headers/music.png)
### When we consider samples, remixes, interpolations, and covers as musical family ties, we can trace how the DNA of one song can spread across genres and cultures. We can see how very different songs might actually be related.
Let’s return to the lineage between “In the Hall of the Mountain King” and “Big Poppa.”
Visual description: A vertical chain retraces the path from In the Hall of the Mountain King to Big Poppa.
The descendants of “In the Hall of the Mountain King” include Jhene Aiko’s The Worst The Worst, a great-great-great grandchild of “In the Hall of the Mountain King” due to a shared lineage with “Big Poppa.”
Visual description: The vertical chain extends from In the Hall of the Mountain King through a shared lineage with Big Poppa, eventually reaching The Worst by Jhené Aiko.
But if we take a different route through the family tree, we can even see “In the Hall of the Mountain King” make its way to Korean rap in J-Hope’s song “What if…”
Visual description: The vertical chain follows an alternate route from In the Hall of the Mountain King to What if by J-Hope, tracing a lineage that spans from classical music to Korean rap.
Doug E. Fresh samples the familiar riff from Inspector Gadget.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues as The Show by Doug E. Fresh & The Get Fresh Crew builds on the riff from Inspector Gadget, blending it into a new hip-hop classic.
Slick Rick’s lyrics are then copied by Big Daddy Kane on “Show & Prove.”
Visual description: The vertical chain continues as Show & Prove by Big Daddy Kane echoes lyrics from The Show
Ol' Dirty Bastard then repeats his own lyrics on “Shimmy Shimmy Ya.”
Visual description: The vertical chain continues with Shimmy Shimmy Ya by Ol’ Dirty Bastard.
J-Hope reinterprets the riff from “Shimmy Shimmy Ya” on the track “What if…”
Visual description: The vertical chain concludes with What if... by j-hope.
The branch to “What if...” is just one of the many, many cousins of “Hit ’Em Up” within “In the Hall of the Mountain King’s” family tree.
If we zoom out, we can see them all, and how “In The Hall of the Mountain King” affects music across 5 generations and 833 songs.
Visual description: The view zooms out to reveal a vast, circular web of 833 songs, with highlighted branches tracing the path from In the Hall of the Mountain King to both What if... and Hit 'Em Up.
The connections in these musical family trees may be a borrowed beat, loaned lyrics, or a multipurpose melody.
Let’s look at examples of each one.
![Image 6: A stylized title for the Borrowed beats section.](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/headers/beats.png)
Some songs have introduced beats that have directly been sampled by hundreds, or even thousands, of other songs.
Depicted here are a small fraction of songs that sample or interpolate James Brown’s 1970 track “Funky Drummer,” which is used in everything from George Michael’s Freedom! '90 Freedom! '90, to Alanis Morissette’s Head Over Feet Head Over Feet, to Ed Sheeran’s Shirtsleeves Shirtsleeves.
And once you hear it, you’ll hear it everywhere; the “Funky Drummer” has been used in thousands of songs and has the most “descendants” in music history.
Visual description: A towering cascade of connections flows from James Brown’s Funky Drummer.
Because the beat doesn’t just pass down to one generation.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues from Funky Drummer to South Bronx by Boogie Down Productions.
It leads “South Bronx” to shape the sound of another Bronx artist’s hit.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues as South Bronx influences Jenny from the Block by Jennifer Lopez.
“Jenny From the Block” is only one of a whole second generation of songs that originate from Clyde Stubblefield’s improvised drum break 5 minutes and 35 seconds into “Funky Drummer.” There’s also Will Smith’s Wild Wild West Wild Wild West, The Power The Power by SNAP!, Rub You The Right Way Rub You The Right Way by Johnny Gill.
Visual description: A zoomed-out view of a branching network from Funky Drummer, with highlighted paths tracing second-generation descendants like Jenny From the Block and dozens of other genre-spanning hits.
![Image 7: A stylized title for the Loaned lyrics section.](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/headers/lyrics.png)
While a beat sets the foundation for a song, lyrics are some of the most easily transmittable DNA: a few words can easily fit into otherwise very different songs.
Here's an example of lyrics slightly evolving through generations: A Tribe Called Quest released “Can I Kick It?” in 1990, itself a song built on Lou Reed’s “Walk on the Wild Side” from 1972. When Q-Tip asks if he can kick it, the rest of the Tribe responds.
Visual description: A vertical chain begins with Can I Kick It? by A Tribe Called Quest.
Robbie Williams then used the line in 2000’s “Rock DJ.” Williams [said](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BnaPtu2sshs) he, “Really struggled to write the lyrics. So what I’ve just done is I’ve robbed loads of really old rap lyrics.”
But instead of his own band responding, it now sounds like the DJ’s crowd.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues to Rock DJ by Robbie Williams.
In 2021, Lorde picked up the line [from](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=If-VG2s0lX8) Robbie Williams— not A Tribe Called Quest—but she takes on both parts.
Visual description: The vertical chain reaches Solar Power by Lorde.
The structure of a catchy phrase can also produce variations with different content altogether.
Tupac also used the phrase “I keep my mind on my money, money on my mind” in a verse on MC Breed’s 1993 Gotta Get Mine Gotta Get Mine, but it blew up when Snoop Dogg quoted it in the chorus of “Gin and Juice” later that year.
Visual description: A branching chain from Snoop Dogg’s Doggystyle to songs by Rihanna and Demi Lovato.
Demi Lovato’s “Cool for the Summer” (2015) plays with that line, but shifts the focus in a different direction…
Visual description: The vertical chain continues from Snoop Dogg’s Gin and Juice to Demi Lovato’s Cool for the Summer.
While Rihanna’s “Cheers (Drink to That)” from 2010, in addition to heavily sampling Avril Lavigne’s “I’m With You,” abandons the parallel format entirely…
Visual description: The vertical chain also leads to Cheers (Drink to That) by Rihanna.
Or the words can stay exactly the same, but completely change meaning.
Chubby Checker popularized the phrase “How low can you go” when he added vocals to The Champs’ song “Limbo Rock.” He’s asking about how far to lower the limbo stick…
Visual description: The vertical chain follows the phrase “How low can you go” from its limbo origins in Limbo Rock to new meanings in tracks by Public Enemy, Ludacris, and Charley Crockett.
But then Chuck D uses the line to talk about the bass singing register.
Visual description: The vertical chain continues to Bring the Noise by Public Enemy.
Ludacris then samples Chuck D’s voice from “Bring the Noise” and alters the tempo and quality to kick off his 2010 song “How Low,” where he’s talking about “booty.”
Visual description: The vertical chain continues to How Low by Ludacris.
While we don’t know which lyric inspired Charley Crockett for his 2019 record “How Low Can You Go,” Crockett used the phrase to describe what a romantic interest is doing to his heart.
Visual description: The vertical chain lands on How Low Can You Go by Charley Crockett.
![Image 8: A stylized title for the Multipurpose melodies section.](https://pudding.cool/2025/04/music-dna/assets/headers/melodies.png)
For most people, however, melody is the most identifiable kind of musical DNA. Sampled and interpolated melodies may be instantly recognizable, hit on a subconscious familiarity even if you’re not aware there’s a sample at all, or sit right at the edge of recognition, making you think “where have I heard that before?”
While sampling is commonly associated with hip hop, the art of sharing and borrowing melodies is a global practice, transcending every genre.
For example, where does this international selection of hits get their sound?
Visual description: Four modern songs—Shaky Shaky by Daddy Yankee, Freaks by French Montana, Post to Be by Omarion, and Labios Mordidos by Kali Uchis and Karol G —are arranged in a horizontal row.
The immediate answer is the 1992 classic “Murder She Wrote” by Chaka Demus and Pliers.
Visual description: A visual tree forms showing the influence of Murder She Wrote by Chaka Demus & Pliers (1992) on the four modern songs.
But “Murder She Wrote” is actually only one of many songs based on a sound from 1973. The bouncing melody behind the song comes from a “riddim”—the instrumental pattern in reggae and dancehall music—that emerged from the song “Stalag 17.”
Visual description: The visual tree shows the instrumental lineage from Stalag 17 by Dave & Ansel Collins (1973) down to Murder She Wrote by Chaka Demus & Pliers (1992), which then branches to the four modern songs.
The “Stalag Riddim” and its descendants form the basis for countless Jamaican hits, including “Murder She Wrote” and Sister Nancy’s “Bam Bam.”
Visual description: The tree highlights how the "Stalag Riddim" from Stalag 17 by Dave & Ansel Collins (1973) leads to Bam Bam by Sister Nancy (1982). Below, Murder She Wrote by Chaka Demus & Pliers (1992) and the four modern songs
Descendants of “Bam Bam” include songs like Do to Me Do to Me by H.E.R., Lost Ones Lost Ones by Lauryn Hill, and Bam Bam by Jay-Z and Damian Marley.
Once a melody enters our musical family in this way, the original source can fade into obscurity, even as the sound continues to pass on and evolve. The descendents of this current generation of songs will build on a melody that a few Jamaican studio musicians recorded in 1973, even if they’ve never given them a second of thought.
Visual description: The tree then traces the influence of Stalag 17 through Bam Bam to three newer songs: Do to Me by H.E.R. (2020), Bam by JAY-Z (2017), and Lost Ones by Lauryn Hill (1998).
# Not your grandparents’ samples
Sampling has become so widespread and so sophisticated, that you can have hits that not only have a wide range of ancestors—they also actually sound like those ancestors. Artists and producers can create incredibly complex and catchy sounds, drawing from a wide range of sources.
Let’s look at the song “Shake It” by Kay Flock featuring Cardi B, Dougie B, and Bory 300. This sample heavy song took off on TikTok before it was even released, and then was one of the New York Times’ top songs of 2022.
Visual description: A visual tree that traces the musical influences behind Shake It by Kay Flock, Cardi B & Dougie B (2022), dividing them into three source tracks: melody from Temperature by Sean Paul, lyrics from Bananza (Belly Dancer) by Akon, and bass from Is Ya Ready by Kay Flock.
In just this segment, there’s a tune from Buffalo Springfield Buffalo Springfield and Fun Boy Three Fun Boy Three, background vocals from Akon’s Bananza Bananza, a clap beat from Sean Paul’s Temperature Temperature and an earlier riddim, and a bass line from a previous Kay Flock song Is Ya Ready Is Ya Ready, all combined together.
The song, produced by Elias Beats, also represents how generational and cross-genre sampling has been turbocharged. Beatmakers like Elias Beats now produce sample-based beats and post them online for free for anyone to build a song around. His YouTube channel has drill beats built around everything from [“Hips Don’t Lie”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x1e4FEaU2xk) to “Just Dance” to [“I Want it That Way”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MyjCpyYgs40) or [“Gangnam Style.”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CjqaJjZ1zSY) Diverse musical DNA from all kinds of traditions and genres are being mixed up and spread out in new and surprising ways.
Then again–there’s something to sticking to the classics, too.
Visual description: A vertical chain connects Ice Ice Baby by Vanilla Ice to Bops Goin Brazy by Tyga.
Methodology To build this project, we used the dataset of hundreds of thousands of songs on Genius.com accessible through their API, over 200,000 of which were “connected” in some way by sample, interpolation, cover, or remix. We used this dataset to identify promising examples and then confirmed or revised the relationships in those examples based on cross-checking with other sources, including WhoSampled.com, Spotify, and news media and academic scholarship. The financial, legal, and reputational implications of sampling and interpolation mean that while reproducing or imitating sound is sometimes formally acknowledged by artists, many others times it is not. The connections we propose here are our interpretation, based on one or more of acknowledged credits by the artists, third-party interpretation, or the sonic evidence available to us.Thank you to DJ LoBraico, Ben Talmi, Josh Katz, and Larry Buchanan for sharing some of their technical and musical skill with this project.
